6.title: Try lots of things. You don't need to pick one.

paragraphs: Join a club, try a sport, pick up an instrument, sign up for something at the library. Say yes to invitations. The goal isn't finding "the thing" yet; it's finding out what you like and don't like. Nothing in 6th grade goes on any future application, so if you try something and hate it, that's useful information. Drop it and try the next thing.

6.title: Read something you actually chose, most days

paragraphs: About 20 minutes a day, on anything genuinely interesting to you: comics, sports stats, fantasy novels, whatever. This is the one 6th-grade habit that quietly compounds for years. It shows up later in reading comprehension, in how standardized tests feel, and eventually in how easily a college essay comes together. It matters far more that you picked the book than what the book is.

6.title: If a subject grabs you, go a little deeper, but only if you want to

paragraphs: Some 6th graders discover they love math, or a particular science, or want to read everything about one topic. If that's you, it's fine to ask a teacher for a harder problem or look for material beyond grade level. This is entirely optional. Just as many students don't know what they're into yet at 11 or 12, and that's just as normal.

6.title: Talk with a parent or guardian about the future, not necessarily 'college'

paragraphs: This doesn't need to be a college conversation specifically. It can be about what your family hopes for you, what kind of work or life feels meaningful, or what your parents' own path looked like, wherever that was. Starting this conversation now, casually and more than once rather than as a single Big Talk, makes it far less loaded later. It also lets parents share their own goals for you, not just hear yours.

6.title: Have a good summer. That's genuinely the assignment.

paragraphs: Skip the "summer program" pressure entirely. A great 6th-grade summer looks like seeing friends, being outside, reading whatever you want, and, only if something sounds fun, a free or low-cost class through the library or a rec center. If you're one of the kids who loves math or another subject, downtime is a fine time to get a little ahead on your own terms — not because it's expected. There's no real disadvantage to a summer that's just a normal, good summer.

7.title: Start noticing what you actually enjoy

paragraphs: By now you've probably tried a handful of things. Notice which ones you look forward to versus which feel like a chore. You don't have to commit to one activity yet, but this is a good year to narrow from "everything" down to the one or two things you actually like.

7.title: Keep reading, and start noticing what subjects pull you in

paragraphs: Keep the daily-reading habit going. Start paying attention to which classes you find yourself curious about, even outside of homework. This isn't about choosing a future major (nowhere close to that yet); it's just about noticing. It'll make choosing electives in 8th and 9th grade easier.

7.title: If a small leadership chance comes up, try it, but don't force it

paragraphs: Something like a club role or a small team responsibility. Early leadership experience is genuinely hard to fabricate later, but this is a "try it if it comes up" note, not a requirement. Plenty of strong students find leadership later, in high school.

7.title: Just learn that 'financial aid' and 'scholarship' exist

paragraphs: No action needed yet. Just knowing these exist matters more than it sounds. Families who don't know financial aid is a thing sometimes rule out colleges based on the listed price alone, years before it would actually matter.

7.title: Keep it low-pressure: reading, friends, maybe a first small job

paragraphs: Same spirit as 6th grade summer. No formal program required. If you're old enough and interested, a first small job or volunteer role (babysitting, yard work, helping at a family business) is a nice, age-appropriate way to build habits, but it's an option, not an expectation.

8.title: Choose your 9th grade classes carefully. This is where your real transcript starts.

paragraphs: This is the first genuinely consequential academic decision in this whole roadmap. Talk to a counselor about which classes, especially any Honors-level options, make sense for you. If your school holds a course-selection night for incoming freshmen, go, and bring a parent if you can. This is often where course-track decisions quietly get made, and it's much easier to start on the right track than to switch onto it later.

8.title: Pick 1–2 activities to carry with you into high school

paragraphs: Consistency reads as genuine interest rather than resume-building, and it's just easier to keep momentum on something you already know you like.

8.title: If a parent didn't attend a U.S. high school, walk through what 9th grade will look like together

paragraphs: Demystify the invisible knowledge — GPA, electives, how grading actually works — before it starts, so it doesn't all land in the first month of 9th grade.

There's no cramming that helps here. Talk to older students or siblings about what 9th grade is actually like. Rest. High school is a bigger adjustment socially than academically for most students, and that's the thing worth being ready for.

This is where the roadmap picks up real pace, on purpose. One idea runs through this whole section starting in 9th grade, so it's worth naming up front: research made public during the 2018 Harvard admissions trial found that applicants with one clear area of real depth (a "spike") were admitted at meaningfully higher rates than similarly qualified "well-rounded" applicants with no standout area. That doesn't mean a single narrow interest is required for every student or every college. Most colleges in the country are far less selective than the schools that data was about, and a well-rounded, engaged student is never a weak applicant. It's just a genuinely useful lens, so it threads through the content below instead of sitting in one place.

9.title: This is the first year that counts, so build the habits now

paragraphs: Every grade from 9th grade on appears on the transcript colleges eventually see. That doesn't mean panic. It means this is the right time to build the study habits, organization, and help-seeking behavior that make the next three years easier, instead of trying to build them under pressure junior year.

GPA (Grade Point Average) is the single number, usually on a 4.0 scale, that summarizes grades across every class. An A is generally worth 4.0, a B a 3.0, and so on, averaged across every semester. Colleges look at both the number and the difficulty of the classes behind it; a solid GPA in a rigorous course load is generally viewed more favorably than a perfect GPA in the easiest available classes. The habit worth building freshman year isn't "get straight A's at all costs." It's learning what to do the moment a grade starts slipping: talk to the teacher, ask about extra help or a retake, adjust a study routine. Students who build that habit now rarely need it in crisis mode junior year.

Just as important this year: meet your school counselor at least once, even just to introduce yourself. Counselors write recommendation letters and flag opportunities later, but generally only for students they actually know, and 9th grade is a low-stakes, no-pressure time to start that relationship. A two-minute hallway conversation or a single scheduled check-in is enough. The goal is just to not be a stranger by junior year, when that relationship starts to matter for real.

9.title: Get to know your school's specific course system now, not later

paragraphs: Every high school structures its course levels a little differently. Some have a clear Honors/AP ladder starting freshman year, others introduce advanced tracks later, and some use different names entirely (IB, dual enrollment, college-in-the-high-school programs). Ask your counselor directly: what's the most rigorous path available to me, and what would it take to move onto it if I'm not on it now? This question comes up every year from here on, so it's worth understanding the actual system at your specific school once, rather than re-guessing it each spring based on rumors from other students. If your school offers dual enrollment (classes that count for both high school and college credit, often at a local community college), it's worth knowing this exists even if you're not ready to use it yet. Some students start using it as early as sophomore year.

9.title: Start a running list of grades, activities, and awards now

paragraphs: A simple notes app works fine. This single habit saves hours of stressful reconstruction junior year, when students are often asked to remember four years of activities from memory while also drafting essays and filling out applications. A good running list has four things worth tracking as you go: what the activity or award was, roughly how many hours a week or per year it took, what you actually did (not just the title), and what you got out of it. That last one is the part people skip and regret skipping. Two years from now, "why did this matter to me" is much harder to reconstruct than "what did I do."

9.title: Join with intention, and start noticing your own 'spike'

paragraphs: This is the year to move from "trying everything" (middle school) to genuinely investing in one or two things. Depth matters more than a long list of one-semester activities. A student who stuck with two things and grew within them almost always presents better than one with ten shallow entries.

If a job, family caregiving responsibility, or translating for parents already takes up real time, that counts as a real activity, not something to hide because it isn't a formal school club. It often demonstrates more maturity and responsibility than a typical extracurricular does. This is also the year to start loosely noticing what your spike might be: the one thing you keep coming back to, whether that's a subject, a skill, a cause, or a craft. Nothing needs to be decided yet. The only job in 9th grade is paying attention to the pattern, not forcing one.

9.title: A note on balance, if school isn't your only responsibility

paragraphs: For a lot of students, and this shows up especially often in immigrant households, "extracurriculars" competes directly with real responsibilities: a part-time job that helps with family income, watching younger siblings after school, translating at appointments. If that's your situation, the honest advice isn't "find time for more activities anyway." It's this: what you're already doing counts, it's real, and it belongs on the running list above exactly like a club would. The instinct to feel behind because your activity list looks thinner than a classmate's is common and not accurate. Depth and responsibility read as strength, not as an excuse.

9.title: Keep the family conversation going, now with real stakes starting to show

paragraphs: The general "what does the future look like" conversation from middle school can get more specific now. This is a good year to talk honestly, as a family, about what feels possible, not to make any decisions yet, but so nobody is operating on assumptions. A few things worth actually saying out loud, even if the answers are "we don't know yet": what a parent hopes for, what a student is starting to want for themselves (which may be different), and roughly what the family's financial reality is, in plain terms a 14- or 15-year-old can understand. If your family's immigration status is something the student doesn't fully understand yet — for example, whether everyone in the household has the same status, or whether that could affect financial aid down the road — this is a reasonable year to start that conversation gently, at whatever pace the family is comfortable with. Nothing needs to be decided or disclosed outside the family. It just helps for the student to know the real shape of the situation before junior year, when it starts to intersect with real decisions. This isn't the year to lock in a plan. It's the year to make sure everyone's talking about the real situation instead of guessing at each other's expectations.

A new activity, a first summer job, or simply more time with the interest you noticed during the school year. Nothing here needs to be impressive yet. This is genuinely the lowest-stakes summer of high school. If you have zero idea what to do with the summer, "get a part-time job" and "go deeper on the one activity you liked most this year" are both completely sufficient answers. This is not the summer that needs a resume-building program.

10.title: Find out what your target schools actually require. This changes school by school.

paragraphs: This is one of the most misunderstood parts of the whole process, and it changed a lot in the past couple of years, so it's worth being precise. As of 2026, the large majority of four-year colleges and universities in the country, over 90% by most tracking organizations' counts, remain test-optional or test-free, meaning the SAT/ACT isn't required. But a meaningful group of highly selective schools reversed course starting in 2024 and now require scores again, including most of the Ivy League, MIT, Caltech, Stanford, and Georgetown, along with the entire Florida and Georgia public university systems. Meanwhile, the University of California system remains test-blind. It won't consider scores even if submitted, no matter how selective the individual UC campus is.

The bottom line: there's no single national rule anymore, and it keeps shifting year to year even at the same school. Whatever a friend, an older sibling, or an old article says about a specific school's policy should be double-checked directly on that school's admissions site before making any decisions about test prep.

International students and students without a Social Security Number sometimes run into extra friction at test registration (the College Board and ACT both have separate international registration processes, and fee waivers work a little differently). If that's your situation, it's worth checking the specific registration requirements early rather than assuming the standard U.S. process applies, so a paperwork surprise doesn't cost you a test date later.

Most sophomores also take the PSAT this year through their school, usually at no cost. It's worth knowing this is a practice run with zero stakes. It doesn't go on any application and doesn't count toward anything yet. Its only real job this year is giving you a sense of the test format and a baseline score, so 11th grade, when the PSAT actually does matter for National Merit consideration, isn't the first time you've seen it.

10.title: Start looking around, with zero pressure to decide anything

paragraphs: Look at 5–10 schools across a real range of selectivity, not to build a final list yet, just to get a feel for size, location, campus type, and vibe. Two free tools worth knowing about: the U.S. Department of Education's College Navigator, and each college's own "Common Data Set" (usually findable by searching the school's name plus "common data set"). Both give real, unfiltered numbers — acceptance rates, average test scores, cost — straight from the source rather than through a ranking site's spin. This is also a good year to notice which schools consistently show up on "affordable for families like mine" lists versus which don't, without committing to anything. If a campus visit is realistic for a school nearby, even an informal one (not an official tour) can tell you more about whether a place feels right than any brochure.

10.title: Go deeper on the thing you noticed last year

paragraphs: If 9th grade was about noticing a pattern, 10th grade is about doing something real with it. A passion project, meaning a self-directed piece of work connected to that interest and sustained over months rather than a single weekend, is one of the most credible ways to show genuine depth, and it doesn't require money or a prestigious program to be real.

Examples that count: teaching yourself a skill and documenting the process, starting a small tutoring effort for younger students, organizing something in a cultural or religious community group, building something (an app, a piece of art, a small business), or doing sustained independent research on a question that actually interests you. What makes a passion project credible isn't prestige. It's that it's sustained, it produces something real, and it's genuinely yours, not something a parent or consultant built for you to present. If a formal summer program or internship also interests you, genuine engagement with a free or low-cost option is valued just as much as an expensive "prestige" program. Ask about fee waivers if cost is the only thing in the way.

10.title: Consider a leadership role, or create one if none exists

paragraphs: By sophomore year, a lot of students start looking for some kind of leadership but assume it has to mean an official title like club president. It doesn't. If your school doesn't have a club around something you care about, starting one is itself a leadership story, and often a more memorable one than inheriting an existing title. If a formal role isn't realistic because of time, cost, or access, organizing something informally (a study group, a small community event, mentoring a younger student one-on-one) counts just as much in how colleges actually read "leadership." What matters is being able to describe, specifically, a time you saw something that needed doing and did it, not the word on a certificate.

10.title: Look up the Net Price Calculator on 2–3 schools you're curious about

paragraphs: Every college is required by law to have one on its website. It takes a few minutes and gives a realistic estimate of what your specific family would actually pay after aid, which is often dramatically different from the sticker price and is a far more useful number to know this early than the listed tuition figure. One honest caveat: Net Price Calculators generally assume a standard financial aid situation, and results can be less accurate for families with a non-citizen parent, self-employment income, or an undocumented household member. If that's your family, treat the number as a rough starting point, not a guarantee, and use the 11th-grade financial aid item below to dig into your specific situation before it matters.

10.title: Start a scholarship radar now, even though it feels early

paragraphs: Most students don't start looking for outside scholarships until senior year, which means they miss two full years of opportunities. Some scholarships are open to underclassmen specifically, and starting a search habit now, even a loose one, means senior year isn't the first time you're figuring out how this works. A simple version of "starting now": ask your counselor if the school keeps a running list of local scholarships (most do), and take five minutes to skim it once a semester. Nothing needs to be applied for yet. The goal this year is just knowing the resource exists so it's not a scramble later.

10.title: A useful check-in: what's changed since last year's conversation?

paragraphs: A short version of the 9th grade family conversation, revisited. Has anything shifted in what a student wants, in the family's situation, in what feels realistic? These don't need to be long conversations, and they work better as a habit (once a year, casually) than as one heavy sit-down. The goal is just making sure the family's mental picture stays current as things genuinely change year to year.
**Summer after 10th Grade — the most important summer for exploration**

Pursue something real: a job, an internship, a summer program, or continued work on a self-directed project. Genuine engagement with what's actually available to you matters more than prestige. A real, sustained commitment to a free program beats passive attendance at an expensive one. If a paid program is the right fit but cost is the barrier, ask directly about fee waivers before ruling it out.

11.title: Lock in your testing plan, or your no-testing plan

paragraphs: If any target schools require or recommend testing, plan for a first attempt by spring of junior year, leaving room for a retake in the fall of senior year if needed. If every school on your list is test-blind or genuinely test-optional and you'd rather not test, not testing is a completely legitimate path. This is a real strategic choice now, not a fallback.

For students who do test: the PSAT taken in October of junior year is the one that actually counts for something. It's the qualifying score for National Merit recognition, a real distinction some colleges give scholarship money for. It's worth taking seriously, but it's not something to prep for separately from the SAT; the two tests overlap enough that general SAT/ACT prep covers it. Also worth knowing: most colleges "superscore," meaning they take your best section scores across multiple test dates rather than just your best single sitting, which is part of why a spring junior-year attempt plus a fall senior-year retake is a common, low-stress pattern rather than treating any one test date as make-or-break. Free, high-quality prep exists (Khan Academy's SAT prep is built directly with the College Board and costs nothing), so a paid course is a choice, not a requirement.

Either way, this is also the year course rigor really starts to matter for the transcript colleges will eventually see in full. Continuing to take the most challenging classes you can handle well remains the single best academic move available.

11.title: Build a real range: reach, target, and safety

paragraphs: A reach school is one where admission is a stretch given your profile. A target is a realistic, competitive fit. A safety should be a school you're confident you'd get into, and this is the part people skip, one you'd genuinely be happy to attend, not just a backup you'd resent. A list that's all reaches isn't a real list. A reasonable range for most students is somewhere around 6–10 schools total, spread across all three categories, though this varies by family circumstances. Cost alone can shrink or reshape the list, and that's a legitimate reason, not a compromise. Revisit the Net Price Calculator numbers from 10th grade for any school on this list. "Can we afford it" is a target/safety-defining question just as much as "will I get in."

11.title: Ask for letters of recommendation the right way

paragraphs: Students should ask teachers at the end of junior year or the very start of senior year, not in the middle of application season when teachers are already juggling dozens of requests. Most schools want two teacher letters, usually from core academic subjects, ideally from teachers who've seen real growth or engagement, not just a high grade.

The single most useful thing a student can do to get a stronger letter is give the teacher a "brag sheet," a short, one-to-two-page document (not the letter itself, just material for the teacher to work from) covering which classes you took with them and when, a specific project or moment in that class you're proud of, why you chose them specifically to write for you, and a few things you'd want a college to understand about you that this teacher is positioned to speak to. This isn't bragging in the way it sounds. It's solving a real problem: a teacher with 150 students genuinely can't remember every specific detail about all of them, and a good brag sheet is the difference between a generic letter and a specific, convincing one. Hand it over at the same time you ask, not weeks later.

11.title: Build a real draft of your activities list this year, not senior fall

paragraphs: The Common App activities list gives about 150 characters per entry to describe what you did. That's tight enough that a strong draft takes real revision, not something to write for the first time under deadline pressure. Junior year is the right time to draft this. For each activity, note what you actually did (specific actions, not just a title), roughly how many hours a week and weeks a year, and any real outcome or impact, however small. A part-time job, a caregiving responsibility, or informal community involvement belongs on this list with the same seriousness as a school club. Colleges read these entries for what a student actually did and learned, not for how official-sounding the title is.

11.title: Start drafting your Common App essay this summer, not during senior fall

paragraphs: The personal essay (250–650 words, answering one of several prompts) isn't a formal writing test. Colleges already have a sense of writing ability from the transcript. Its real job is showing personality and how a student actually thinks, in their own voice.

Brainstorming, not the writing itself, is usually where students get stuck, so it's worth having a real method rather than staring at a blank page. A few that genuinely work: write down five moments that changed how you see something, however small; make a list of the values you'd want a friend to describe you by, then find a specific memory attached to each one; or literally tell your story out loud to a friend who wasn't there, the way you'd naturally tell it, then write down what you actually said. Most strong essays fall into one of two shapes: a Narrative structure, built around a single specific scene or turning point, or a Montage structure, connecting a few smaller moments through one throughline. Either can work well. What matters more is picking one and committing to it rather than trying to cover everything.

One note worth saying directly, since a lot of PathFinder's audience has a version of this story available to write: an essay about immigrating, translating for parents, or family hardship is completely valid material. It's real and it matters. But admissions readers see an enormous number of essays that hit the same broad beats in the same broad way, and a broad version of a real story can accidentally read as generic. The fix isn't avoiding the topic. It's the opposite: going more specific, not less. The particular smell of a specific waiting room. The exact sentence a grandmother said. The precise moment a translation went wrong in a way only you would know about. Specific, small, and true beats sweeping and general almost every time, on this topic and every other one.

Starting a rough draft the summer before senior year, while there's no application deadline pressure yet, is the single biggest stress-reducer available for the fall. Plan on 4–6 real drafts, not one polished attempt. That's normal, not a sign something's wrong. A parent's most useful role is protecting the time and quiet needed to write an honest draft, and reading for clarity and grammar at the end, not suggesting the topic or rewriting the substance. Admissions readers can usually tell when an adult's voice replaced a student's.

11.title: Research your family's specific situation now, before application season adds pressure

paragraphs: This is a good year to actually name your family's situation and find out what it means, rather than guessing. A few concrete starting points depending on what applies to you: if any parent is a non-citizen, you can still file the FAFSA as the student (the student's own citizenship status is what determines eligibility, not the parents'), and the form has a specific path for parents without a Social Security Number. If your family includes an undocumented member, that alone doesn't disqualify a U.S. citizen or eligible student from federal aid, though state-level aid rules vary a lot and are worth checking specifically for your state. If a student is themselves undocumented or has DACA status, federal aid generally isn't available, but a growing number of states offer state financial aid or in-state tuition regardless of federal status, and this is genuinely worth researching by name for your state rather than assuming the answer. If a family runs a small business or has self-employment income, that income gets reported differently on aid forms and is worth understanding ahead of time rather than during a rushed filing. None of this needs to be figured out alone. A school counselor or a nonprofit that works with immigrant families can walk through your specific situation, and doing that now, while there's time to ask a question and wait for a real answer, avoids discovering a complication in the middle of application season when everything else is also due. (See the Financial Aid and Immigrant Families guide articles for the current rules on exactly this.)

11.title: Turn scholarship awareness into a real, systematic search

paragraphs: The single biggest mistake in scholarship searching is treating it as a one-time event: sitting down once, browsing a database for twenty minutes, bookmarking a few things, and never following through. New scholarships post constantly and deadlines are scattered across the whole year, not clustered in the spring the way most students assume. A search that actually works has a few concrete parts. Ask your counselor directly for the school's local scholarship list; this is consistently the highest-value, most underused resource, since local awards have far less competition than national ones. Ask parents whether an employer offers scholarships for employees' children. Check community organizations with a local presence: cultural or religious associations, credit unions, service clubs like Rotary or the Lions Club, immigrant-serving nonprofits. A number of scholarships are specifically restricted to or prioritize first-generation, immigrant, or DACA students; it's worth searching for those by name rather than assuming a general scholarship search will surface them. And set up a simple recurring habit, like one hour a month, rather than trying to do it all at once senior year. Smaller, less-competitive local awards genuinely add up, and are worth real time even though they don't have the headline appeal of a big national scholarship.

11.title: Have the money conversation as a family, specifically now

paragraphs: By junior year, the college list is starting to take real shape, which makes this the right moment for a specific, concrete conversation, not "college is expensive" in the abstract but actual numbers: what the family can realistically contribute, what the Net Price Calculator estimates suggested for schools on the list, and how open the family is to loans versus wanting to avoid them. This conversation is uncomfortable in a lot of households, and doubly so in families where talking openly about money isn't the norm, or where a parent's own unfamiliarity with the U.S. system makes the numbers feel harder to trust. It can help to bring the actual Net Price Calculator results into the conversation as a concrete anchor, rather than talking in generalities. Having this conversation now, calmly and before any decisions are due, is far better than having it under pressure in April of senior year when an offer just arrived and a deposit is due in days.
**Summer after 11th Grade — the most important summer overall**

This is when the Common App essay gets drafted and the college list gets finalized: the single biggest stress-reducer for the fall of senior year, when everything else (supplemental essays, recommendation letter requests, financial aid forms) piles up at once. If only one thing gets done this summer, make it the essay draft. Everything else on this year's list is more flexible than that one is.

12.title: Avoid senioritis. Your spring grades still matter more than it feels like they do.

paragraphs: It's genuinely common, after months of pressure, to want to coast once acceptances start arriving. But colleges don't receive final grades until the summer, and a real drop, not a single B but a pattern like A's and B's turning into C's and D's, can lead a college to ask for an explanation, place a student on academic probation, reduce a merit scholarship tied to GPA, or in rare but real cases, rescind the offer outright. Because colleges don't see the final transcript until June or July, a student might not find out about a problem until after they've already turned down every other school. The safe target isn't perfection. It's not letting a real pattern develop. If a genuine hardship is behind a grade drop, telling the college proactively, rather than waiting for them to notice, tends to go better.

12.title: Submit the FAFSA, and CSS Profile if required, as early as your family reasonably can

paragraphs: The FAFSA generally opens each fall, and some aid is awarded first-come, first-served, so earlier is better once your family has what it needs to file accurately. As of the 2026–27 cycle, the process itself is faster than it's been in years: the form now shows your Student Aid Index and Pell Grant eligibility in real time right after submission, instead of families waiting weeks to find out. If a parent doesn't have a Social Security Number, the FAFSA has a specific process for that (the parent creates an account without one), so don't let that stop you from starting the form. It just means budgeting a little extra time in case that step trips up.

12.title: Build one system to track every school's requirements, portal, and deadline

paragraphs: By senior fall, a student applying to even 6–8 schools is juggling that many separate portals, each with its own login, its own supplemental essay prompts, its own document upload requirements, and its own deadline. Regular Decision, Early Action, and Early Decision dates can all be different even within the same list. A single tracking document (a spreadsheet, a notes app, anything that isn't memory) listing each school, its deadline, what's been submitted, and what's still outstanding is the single easiest way to avoid the specific failure mode that trips up organized, capable students most often: a small supplemental requirement, like a short-answer question, an extra recommendation, or a certification form, buried below the main essay and missed entirely, leaving an otherwise complete application incomplete.

12.title: Pace the supplemental essays. They add up fast.

paragraphs: The Common App essay is one essay written once. Supplemental essays, the shorter, school-specific "why this college" or "why this major" prompts, are written many times, once per school, and this is where senior fall applications actually get heavy. A "why this college" essay that could be copy-pasted between two schools with just the name swapped is a weak one. The strongest version names something specific to that campus (a program, a professor's research area, a tradition) and connects it to something specific about the student. Starting these as soon as the Common App essay is stable, rather than saving all of them for the final weeks before each deadline, is what actually prevents the late-November crunch most seniors describe as the hardest part of the whole process.

12.title: If you're deferred or waitlisted, there's a real, specific thing to do

paragraphs: Being deferred (from an early application, reconsidered in the regular round) or waitlisted (after regular decision) isn't a rejection. A meaningful share of institutions maintain waitlists, and a real number of students are admitted off them each year, though it's not the majority. For a school that's still a genuine top choice, a letter of continued interest, a short, direct communication to that school's admissions office, is worth sending, usually within a couple of weeks of the decision. A good one does three things: reaffirms specifically why this school remains the right fit (not generic praise, something concrete like a program or a person on campus); updates the school on anything genuinely new since the application was submitted (a grade trend, an award, a new project); and if true, states plainly that this school would be the student's clear first choice and they'd enroll immediately if admitted. Schools pay real attention to this signal. What doesn't help: repeating the essay, sounding desperate, or sending more than one letter. Always check the specific school's policy first. Some explicitly discourage extra letters, and that instruction should be followed exactly.

12.title: Read every offer for what's actually in it, not just the total number

paragraphs: Two schools can list the "same" total aid amount while one is mostly grants (free money) and the other is mostly loans (money repaid later, with interest). Those are very different offers in real terms. As of the 2026–27 award year, a few federal rules changed that are worth knowing before comparing offers: Parent PLUS loans now carry a $20,000 annual cap and a $65,000 lifetime cap per student, and having multiple children in college at the same time no longer reduces your calculated Student Aid Index the way it used to under the old formula. It's also worth knowing about "scholarship displacement." Some colleges reduce their own institutional aid when a student brings in an outside scholarship, while others don't. This varies by school and is worth a direct question to the financial aid office before assuming an outside scholarship is pure extra money.

12.title: Compare offers using one real method, not just a gut feeling about the total

paragraphs: Award letters are written inconsistently on purpose. Different schools use different terms for the same things, and some list loans right alongside grants in a way that makes the "total aid" number misleading. One method that works: for each school, write down the full Cost of Attendance (tuition, fees, housing, food, the real total, not just tuition), then subtract only the grants and scholarships, never the loans, to get the actual out-of-pocket cost before borrowing. A school that looks cheaper only because it offered more loans isn't actually cheaper. It's the same cost, deferred, with interest added. Comparing that one number, Cost of Attendance minus real gift aid, across every offer is the closest thing to an apples-to-apples comparison, and it's worth doing before any conversation about which school "feels" more affordable.

12.title: Keep applying for outside scholarships through the spring. This isn't just a fall task.

paragraphs: A lot of students stop searching for scholarships the moment college applications are submitted, but plenty of scholarship deadlines fall in the winter and spring of senior year, some specifically for students who already have an acceptance in hand. Local scholarships in particular, through community foundations, cultural or religious organizations, employer programs, and civic groups, tend to have smaller applicant pools than national ones, which means genuinely better odds for the time invested, even though the awards themselves are usually smaller. It adds up.

12.title: If an offer feels insufficient, know that appealing is normal, not a last resort

paragraphs: Colleges expect and accommodate appeals, especially with a specific, documented change in circumstances (job loss, a new medical expense, a sibling starting college) or a meaningfully better offer from a comparable school. Contact the financial aid office directly and ask about their appeal or reconsideration process. Most have a real one, even when it isn't advertised prominently. Timing matters here: most families have offers in hand by early-to-mid March, which leaves a real window to appeal before the May 1 decision deadline most schools use. Waiting until the last week rarely leaves enough time for a school to respond.

12.title: Choosing between offers: a framework, not just the name that sounds most impressive

paragraphs: It's worth saying plainly: research on long-term career satisfaction and wellbeing has consistently found that a school's prestige matters far less than commonly assumed. What actually predicts a good outcome is closer to whether a student found professors and mentors who engaged with them and real chances to apply what they were learning, and those things exist at colleges across every tier of selectivity, not just the most famous names. A more useful comparison than "which name is better" is a short, honest list, side by side for each real option: the true out-of-pocket cost (from the method above), how it felt on a visit or through direct research if a visit wasn't possible, whether the specific program or major of interest is genuinely strong there, and how realistic the location and size feel day to day. Slowing down and comparing on these terms, rather than reacting to the first acceptance that arrives, tends to produce a decision a student feels better about a year later.

12.title: Understand what a deposit actually means, and the May 1 deadline

paragraphs: Most colleges use May 1, sometimes called National College Decision Day, as the deadline to accept an offer and pay an enrollment deposit, though Early Decision applicants commit earlier and some schools set their own dates, so it's worth checking each school directly rather than assuming May 1 applies everywhere. The deposit itself is usually non-refundable and holds a spot in the incoming class. Not paying it by the deadline generally means losing that spot. "Double depositing," paying deposits at two schools at once to buy more time to decide, is against the guidelines most colleges follow and carries real risk (both offers can be rescinded if discovered), so the right approach is committing to one school by the deadline, even if a waitlist decision from another school is still pending elsewhere. If that waitlist offer comes through later, a student can still switch, but the first deposit is generally lost in the process. This is a normal, planned-for cost of keeping options open, not a sign anything went wrong.
